beats.text: In 1781, a British army under Lord Cornwallis was marching through Virginia. An American army under a young French general, the Marquis de Lafayette, was trying to stop it.

overlays.hook: The spy who helped win Yorktown.

beats.text: Lafayette needed to know what the British were planning.

visual.caption: The Marquis de Lafayette, 1782

beats.text: One of the men he relied on was enslaved. His name was James.

visual.caption: James Lafayette, portrait by John B. Martin, 1824

beats.text: James went into the British camp, again and again, and carried what he learned back to Lafayette.
That October, Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown.

visual.caption: The Surrender of Lord Cornwallis, by John Trumbull

beats.text: But when the war was over, James was still enslaved. This is the story of how he won his freedom.

visual.title: Still enslaved
visual.sub: after the war he helped win

beats.text: He never fired a shot. His weapon was what he heard.
James was born around 1748, most likely in New Kent County, Virginia.
He was enslaved by a man named William Armistead.
During the Revolution, Armistead managed military supplies for Virginia.

visual.caption: Williamsburg, York, Hampton and Portsmouth, French map, 1781

beats.text: In 1780, Virginia moved its capital from Williamsburg to Richmond, and James most likely went with Armistead.
That is nearly all we know of his early life. Even his birth year is uncertain. He left no diary, and the records are thin.
Today he is usually called James Armistead Lafayette, after both the family that enslaved him and the general he served.

visual.caption: James Lafayette, portrait by John B. Martin, 1824

beats.text: In 1781, the war came to Virginia.
Benedict Arnold, the American general who had gone over to the British, led raids there from a base at Portsmouth.

visual.caption: Benedict Arnold

beats.text: Then Lord Cornwallis brought his army north into Virginia.

visual.caption: Charles, Lord Cornwallis

beats.text: Facing him was the Marquis de Lafayette, a young French nobleman in command of the Continental Army in Virginia.

visual.caption: The Marquis de Lafayette, major general of the American army, 1782

beats.text: In the summer of 1781, by most accounts with his enslaver's permission, James went to serve Lafayette.
He did not take up arms. On paper he was a servant. In fact, he was a spy.
Most accounts say he posed as a runaway slave, and made his way into the British camp.

visual.caption: Portsmouth, Virginia, French plan, 1781

beats.text: The British needed men who knew the local roads. He guided their troops, earned their trust, and listened.
He reported where the British troops were posted, and what arms they had.
Many accounts go further. They say he became a servant at Cornwallis's own headquarters, and that the British asked him to spy on the Americans.

visual.caption: Lord Cornwallis

beats.text: Lafayette's own letters to George Washington, written in July and August 1781, mention an informant in Cornwallis's camp. They do not give his name.

visual.caption: The Marquis de Lafayette

beats.text: If so, he was a double agent. He brought true reports to Lafayette, and false ones back to the British.

visual.title: Double agent
visual.sub: true reports one way, false ones the other

beats.text: Every trip across the lines was a risk. One wrong word, one letter found, and it would be over.
In late August, Lafayette learned that Cornwallis had moved his army from Portsmouth to Yorktown, on the York River.

visual.caption: Yorktown, French plan of the siege, 1781

beats.text: At Yorktown, with the river at his back, Cornwallis could be trapped by land and by sea.
George Washington and the French general Rochambeau marched south. A French fleet sailed into the Chesapeake Bay.

visual.caption: Washington, Lafayette and Tilghman at Yorktown, by Charles Willson Peale

beats.text: The allied armies dug in around the town, and the siege began.

visual.caption: Soldiers at the siege of Yorktown, sketched by a French officer, 1781

beats.text: For about three weeks, cannon fire pounded the British lines.
On October 19, 1781, Cornwallis surrendered his army.

visual.caption: The surrender at Yorktown, engraving

beats.text: Thousands of British and German soldiers marched out and laid down their arms.

visual.caption: The British surrender at Yorktown, French print, 1781

beats.text: The war was all but won.
How much of the spy story can we prove? Less than the legend.
Historians point out that the surviving papers, his own petition and Lafayette's letter, do not say that he served Cornwallis himself.

visual.caption: Lafayette's 1784 certificate, printed with James's portrait

beats.text: Some of the legend grew later, from a novel and from storytellers who filled in the gaps.
What those papers do say is striking enough.
In his petition, James said he went into the British camp again and again, at the risk of his life, and carried Lafayette's secret messages into enemy lines.

visual.title: At the risk of his life

beats.text: If he had been caught, he could have been executed.
After the war, Virginia passed a law freeing enslaved men who had served as soldiers.
It covered men who had been given a gun and sent to fight, often in their owner's place.
James had not carried a gun. He had been a spy. The law did not cover him, and he stayed enslaved.
On November 21, 1784, Lafayette wrote a certificate for him.

visual.caption: Lafayette's 1784 certificate, printed with James's portrait

beats.text: This is to certify, it began, that the bearer has done essential services to me while I had the honour to command in this State.

visual.quote: This is to certify that the Bearer has done essential services to me while I had the honour to command in this State.

beats.text: His intelligences from the enemy's camp were industriously collected and most faithfully delivered.

visual.quote: His intelligences from the enemy's camp were industriously collected and most faithfully delivered.

beats.text: He appears to me entitled to every reward his situation can admit of.

visual.quote: He appears to me entitled to every reward his situation can admit of.

beats.text: With that letter, James asked the Virginia legislature for his freedom. His first petition failed.
In 1786 he tried again, and this time William Armistead supported him.
His petition, dated November 30, 1786, is still kept at the Library of Virginia.
On January 9, 1787, the act freeing him became law.
Both houses of the Assembly had passed it, and Governor Edmund Randolph signed it.
The state paid William Armistead two hundred fifty pounds for him.
And James chose a last name. Lafayette.

visual.caption: James Lafayette, portrait by John B. Martin, 1824

beats.text: James Lafayette settled in New Kent County, on a farm of about forty acres.

visual.caption: New Kent County, Virginia, today

beats.text: He married, and raised a family.
Records show that he, too, came to own enslaved people. History is rarely simple.
By 1818 he was about seventy, poor and in failing health. He asked the legislature for help.
It gave him sixty dollars at once, and a pension of forty dollars a year.
In 1824, the Marquis de Lafayette came back to America, for a long farewell tour.

visual.caption: The Marquis de Lafayette, 1825

beats.text: The tour lasted more than a year, from July 1824 to September 1825, and took him through all twenty-four states.

visual.caption: A medal struck for Lafayette's visit, 1824

beats.text: Crowds came out wherever he went.

visual.caption: A medal struck for Lafayette's visit, 1824

beats.text: In Virginia, the old general saw James in the crowd. He called him by name, and embraced him.
It was more than forty years after Yorktown.
That same year, an artist named John Blennerhassett Martin painted James's portrait.

visual.caption: James Lafayette, portrait by John B. Martin, 1824

beats.text: It shows him in a dark coat with a white collar. A free man.
Copies were printed together with Lafayette's certificate.

visual.caption: Lafayette's 1784 certificate, printed with James's portrait

beats.text: In 1828, a Virginia novel, Edge Hill, told the story of a spy named James.
James Lafayette died on his farm in 1830.
He went into the enemy camp with nothing but his wits, knowing what would happen if he were caught.
He was born enslaved, served in secret, and was freed by a letter of thanks and an act of the legislature.

visual.caption: Lafayette's 1784 certificate, printed with James's portrait

beats.text: He helped bring about the surrender that won the war. Then he had to fight again, on paper, for his own freedom.
He won it. And he took the name of the man who had vouched for him.

visual.caption: James Lafayette, portrait by John B. Martin, 1824

beats.text: That was James Lafayette. Subscribe for more.

notUsed: Serving Cornwallis himself / the "deception" story (OAR, History.com, Wikipedia) is not confirmed by surviving papers (Journal of the American Revolution): told as "many accounts say", then checked.
Birth year 1748 (OAR, from his 1818 petition) vs 1760 (some sources): script says "around 1748" and "even his birth year is uncertain".
Death 1830 (OAR, Library of Virginia) vs 1832 (some sources): script uses 1830.
Place of the 1824 embrace: Yorktown (OAR, citing the Richmond Enquirer) vs Richmond (Wikipedia): script says "in Virginia".
Le Paon's 1783 "Lafayette at Yorktown" shows an unidentified Black man; often claimed to be James, not confirmed: image not used.
Number of British troops surrendered: not used.
